column2: The Etch A Sketch, the drawing toy with two knobs. PAIR: graphite line #3c3c3c on aluminium-powder grey #c4c4bc (the glass is the toy's screen only; the red frame is off the glass, so knobs, if shown, are drawn in the same two colours inside it). The rule of the medium is its whole charm: everything is drawn by ONE continuous 1-px stylus line that can only move by the two knobs (horizontal and vertical motion, diagonals as staircases, curves as careful knob-twiddled steps), never lifted, so the line must travel from digit to digit and retrace itself. Design the ten numerals as single-line Etch A Sketch drawings (double or triple traced strokes for weight, the characteristic stepped curves, the connecting travel line kept faint by being a single 1-px pass, or hidden by retracing), bold enough at --scale 4, and the line that joins them part of the design (a horizon, a little house, a signature flourish). Constant life: the stylus is always drawing: a little cursor point visible, it doodles in the empty space (a cat, a skyline, a spiral, a maze) at a steady 1-2 px a frame, each doodle partly erased by a gentle tilt (the aluminium powder sliding back as a soft dithered band) before the next; the knobs, if shown, turn with the motion. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the toy is tilted: the old digit fades out evenly as the powder re-coats it (an even dissolve or dither front, never a partial that reads as another digit; gone before :00), and after :00 the stylus races along the new digit's single line, first pass thin over its whole route, then thickening on the retrace. Hour: a bigger show: the whole toy is shaken: the powder sweeps the screen clean in sloshing waves (a dithered band rolling back and forth, the hour digits redrawn quickly behind it so the time is never blank > 1 s), then the stylus draws a grander picture around the time.

Typewriter art (concrete poetry, ASCII art before computers, the 1960s typists who made portraits from x's and o's). PAIR: carbon ribbon ink #1c1c3a on onionskin paper #efe9da. Design your own tiny typewriter typeface (a monospaced slab-serif 'Courier' for this grid: each glyph ~4x6 or 5x7, pixel-designed, with the uneven ink of a real typewriter: occasional faint or doubled strikes rendered as missing or extra pixels, a slight baseline wobble per character), and lay the page on a fixed character grid. The time is TYPED: the numerals are big typewriter-art figures made of characters (8, @, #, M, W for dense ink; o, x, : and . for lighter tones, overstrike for the darkest), so up close they are text and from arm's length they are bold digits (check at --scale 4 that they read as digits, and up close that the characters are crisp). Constant life: the typist is always typing: the carriage moves along a line of a little poem or a weather log beneath or around the time, characters strike one by one with a tiny jump, the bell rings at line end (a visual 'ding' mark), the carriage returns with a smooth slide, the paper feeds up by a line, words get x'd out and retyped. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the old digit is erased the typewriter way (correction tape: each character of the digit overstruck evenly at once into a uniform hatch, then the paper feeds the old figure up and away, gone before :00), and after :00 the new digit is typed: the carriage zips along its rows, striking all its characters in a rhythmic run, row by row but with a light full outline typed first so no partial reads as another digit. Hour: a bigger show: the sheet is pulled out and a fresh sheet rolls in (a smooth scroll), and the typist types a large ornamental hour in typewriter art with a border of repeated characters, the time readable throughout.

The pin art toy and the Alexeieff-Parker pinscreen of 1930s animation: a field of thousands of pins pushed from behind; where they are pushed out their heads catch light, where they are pulled back they sink into shadow. PAIR: pin-head silver #e4e6ea on deep charcoal #202428. Draw the pin field as a 1-bit grid of pin heads (every 2 or 3 px a dot, the pushed-out pins as bigger or lit dots, a flat cast shadow offset to one side as the 1-bit way of showing how far each pin stands out: no shading ramps, only dot size and shadow length), so depth reads as a halftone. The time is PRESSED into the pins: the numerals stand out of the field as raised plateaus of pins (design all ten as bold relief shapes with clean counters, crisp edges in the pin grid, unmistakable at --scale 4). Constant life: the field is alive: slow waves ripple through the free pins like wind over a field (pins rising and falling a step at a time as a travelling wave of dot sizes), a hand or a small object (a key, a shell, a toy car) is pressed in from behind somewhere in the empty space and leaves its impression, which relaxes back over seconds. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the changing digit's pins sink back evenly (all its pins stepping down together, never a partial that reads as another digit; gone before :00), and after :00 a hand presses from behind and the new digit's pins rise, the outline first, then the face, settling with a little overshoot ripple. Hour: a bigger show: the whole board is swept and reset: a wave of pins rolls across the board lifting everything and settling it to reveal a new relief scene around the time (a face, a landscape, a pattern), the hour digits always standing proud.

A tower block at night seen from across the street, its lit windows the pixels. PAIR: lamp-light yellow #ffd23c on night navy #0b1430. The glass is a wall of flats: a grid of windows (each ~3x4 px with mullions; choose a size that reads), the building's edges, balconies, a water tower and antennas on the roof against the sky, all drawn only in yellow (lit) and navy (unlit or dark); the dark building reads by its few lit features. The time is the pattern of lit windows: the numerals are formed by who has their lights on (design ten digits on the window grid as bold, well-proportioned shapes with clean counters, unmistakable at --scale 4; the grid cells may also be split into halves to give curves). Constant life, the 'Rear Window' charm: inside the lit windows tiny navy silhouettes live their lives (one cooks, one dances, a cat walks along a sill, someone draws the curtain halfway, a TV flickers as a tiny dither pattern), a few non-digit windows switch on and off now and then as background (kept dimmer as dithered or half-curtained so they never compete with the time), a lift light moves up the stairwell, a plane's light crosses the sky. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the old digit's residents switch off all together at the same moment window by window but evenly across the digit (never leaving a partial that reads as another digit; gone before :00), and after :00 the new digit's lights come on: a ripple of switches running through the digit's windows quickly, curtains opening. Hour: a bigger show: a blackout and recovery (all non-time windows go dark, then the block lights up floor by floor), or fireworks bloom over the roof in 1-bit sparks while every resident comes to the window, the time readable throughout.
